Inspect and prepare data

Source: vignettes/inspect-and-prepare.Rmd
inspect-and-prepare.Rmd

A course coordinator sends you a survey spreadsheet. Before comparing the centres, you need to understand its columns, clean its measurements and check that the records fit together. This guide introduces that workflow; each function’s reference page covers its additional options.

Find your way around

Here are the twelve participants from Getting started. The two scores are assessment items, and -99 means income was undisclosed.

library(dplyr)
library(tibble)
library(tidystata)

survey <- tribble(
  ~id, ~centre,     ~satisfied, ~income_text, ~score1, ~score2,
    1, "Riverside", "Yes",     "1,200",           2,       4,
    2, "Riverside", "Yes",     "1,500",           4,      NA,
    3, "Riverside", "No",      "",               NA,      NA,
    4, "Riverside", NA,        "-99",             6,       8,
    5, "Riverside", "Yes",     "2,200",           8,      10,
    6, "Riverside", "Yes",     "1,800",           4,       6,
    7, "Hilltop",   "No",      "1,400",           3,       5,
    8, "Hilltop",   "Yes",     "2,100",           5,       7,
    9, "Hilltop",   "No",      "2,600",           7,       9,
   10, "Hilltop",   "Yes",     NA,                9,      NA,
   11, "Hilltop",   "Yes",     "2,300",          NA,       8,
   12, "Hilltop",   NA,        "1,700",           6,       8
) |>
  mutate(score1 = haven::labelled(score1, label = "First assessment item"))

survey |> variables()
#> # A tibble: 6 × 2
#>   name        label                
#>   <chr>       <chr>                
#> 1 id          NA                   
#> 2 centre      NA                   
#> 3 satisfied   NA                   
#> 4 income_text NA                   
#> 5 score1      First assessment item
#> 6 score2      NA

variables() pairs column names with their labels. Search the descriptions when a large file has names that are hard to remember:

survey |> variables_search("assessment")
#> # A tibble: 1 × 2
#>   name   label                
#>   <chr>  <chr>                
#> 1 score1 First assessment item

Use ds() for a vector of matching names, or codebook() for types and counts. The same tidy selection works when inspecting or calculating:

survey |>
  select_or_transmute(id, starts_with("score"), income = destring(income_text))
#> # A tibble: 12 × 4
#>       id score1    score2 income
#>    <dbl> <dbl+lbl>  <dbl>  <dbl>
#>  1     1  2             4   1200
#>  2     2  4            NA   1500
#>  3     3 NA            NA     NA
#>  4     4  6             8    -99
#>  5     5  8            10   2200
#>  6     6  4             6   1800
#>  7     7  3             5   1400
#>  8     8  5             7   2100
#>  9     9  7             9   2600
#> 10    10  9            NA     NA
#> 11    11 NA             8   2300
#> 12    12  6             8   1700

select_or_transmute() combines selecting existing columns and computing new ones. varlist("score*") offers Stata-style wildcard selection; ordinary starts_with() works throughout this guide. For an interactive spreadsheet view, use browse() in your own session.

Clean values before calculating

Read the income strings and replace the sentinel. Use across() to apply a conversion to several columns when needed.

clean <- survey |>
  mutate(income = destring(income_text) |> mvdecode(-99))

clean |> misstable(income, starts_with("score"))
#> # A tibble: 3 × 4
#>   variable miss_n miss_pct valid_n
#>   <chr>     <int>    <dbl>   <int>
#> 1 income        3     25         9
#> 2 score1        2     16.7      10
#> 3 score2        3     25         9

The income column now has three missing values: a blank answer, the sentinel and an original NA. Use na_if_value() for the corresponding single-value replacement. mvencode() and value_if_na() go in the other direction when an export needs a sentinel; keep ordinary NA values for calculations.

Category codes need a different decision. encode() gives text categories labelled integer codes. decode() reads those labels back; tostring() and its alias as_character() instead return the stored codes as text.

clean |>
  mutate(
    centre_code = encode(centre),
    centre_label = decode(centre_code),
    code_text = tostring(centre_code)
  ) |>
  distinct(centre, centre_code, centre_label, code_text)
#> # A tibble: 2 × 4
#>   centre    centre_code   centre_label code_text
#>   <chr>     <int+lbl>     <chr>        <chr>    
#> 1 Riverside 2 [Riverside] Riverside    2        
#> 2 Hilltop   1 [Hilltop]   Hilltop      1

Encode before grouping so all centres share one coding dictionary. Keep exact identifiers as text from import, rather than converting rounded numbers back to strings.

Create measurements inside mutate()

How many assessment items did each participant answer, and what was their average? Row helpers work directly with the columns selected by pick().

prepared <- clean |>
  mutate(
    score = row_mean(pick(score1, score2)),
    answered = row_non_miss(pick(score1, score2)),
    score_z = std(score)
  )

prepared |> select(id, starts_with("score"), answered)
#> # A tibble: 12 × 6
#>       id score1    score2 score score_z answered
#>    <dbl> <dbl+lbl>  <dbl> <dbl>   <dbl>    <int>
#>  1     1  2             4     3  -1.59         2
#>  2     2  4            NA     4  -1.12         1
#>  3     3 NA            NA    NA  NA            0
#>  4     4  6             8     7   0.302        2
#>  5     5  8            10     9   1.25         2
#>  6     6  4             6     5  -0.646        2
#>  7     7  3             5     4  -1.12         2
#>  8     8  5             7     6  -0.172        2
#>  9     9  7             9     8   0.775        2
#> 10    10  9            NA     9   1.25         1
#> 11    11 NA             8     8   0.775        1
#> 12    12  6             8     7   0.302        2

The all-missing participant keeps an NA average. std() expresses the observed averages in sample standard deviations. Related row helpers calculate sums, minima, maxima and missing counts without a rowwise() step.

For a simple reporting band, recode ranges and then display their labels:

prepared |>
  mutate(band = stata_recode(score, Lower = min:5 ~ 1, Higher = 5:max ~ 2)) |>
  fre(band)
#> # A tibble: 5 × 6
#>   band            n percent   cum valid valid_cum
#>   <chr>       <int>   <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>     <dbl>
#> 1 Lower           4   33.3   33.3  36.4      36.4
#> 2 Higher          7   58.3   91.7  63.6     100  
#> 3 Valid Total    11   91.7   NA   100        NA  
#> 4 NA              1    8.33 100    NA        NA  
#> 5 Total          12  100     NA    NA        NA

Rules are applied in order, so a score of exactly 5 belongs to Lower. xtile() makes quantile groups while keeping ties together; cut_breaks() uses chosen boundaries and cut_length() equal-width intervals. For indicator columns, use as_dummy() (also called tab_gen()); its .names option selects value-, index- or label-based names.

Check records before combining them

A participant ID should identify one survey row. isid() confirms the key and passes the data along; assert() checks a condition inside the pipeline.

prepared |>
  isid(id) |>
  assert(is.na(score) | (score >= 0 & score <= 10)) |>
  select(id, score) |>
  print_headtail(n = 4)
#> Variable `id` uniquely identifies the rows.
#> # A tibble: 12 × 2
#>       id score
#>    <dbl> <dbl>
#>  1     1     3
#>  2     2     4
#>  ⋮     ⋮     ⋮
#> 11    11     8
#> 12    12     7
#> # ... 8 rows omitted in the middle; use print(x, n = Inf) to show all rows.

If an import contains repeated records, start with duplicates_report() and inspect them with duplicates_list(). duplicates_tag() marks them, and duplicates_drop() keeps the first after you decide which rows are redundant.

Now attach the number of course sessions offered by each centre. Declare the many-participants-to-one-centre relationship and require a match for every row.

centres <- tribble(
  ~centre,     ~sessions,
  "Riverside",         8,
  "Hilltop",          10
)

prepared |>
  stata_merge(centres, "m:1", by = "centre", assert = "match") |>
  select(id, centre, sessions, .merge) |>
  print_headtail(n = 4)
#> Result                            Rows
#> --------------------------------------
#> Not matched                          0
#>     from master                      0  (.merge == "master only")
#>     from using                       0  (.merge == "using only")
#> 
#> Matched                             12  (.merge == "matched")
#> --------------------------------------
#> # A tibble: 12 × 4
#>       id centre    sessions .merge 
#>    <dbl> <chr>        <dbl> <fct>  
#>  1     1 Riverside        8 matched
#>  2     2 Riverside        8 matched
#>  ⋮     ⋮     ⋮            ⋮    ⋮   
#> 11    11 Hilltop         10 matched
#> 12    12 Hilltop         10 matched
#> # ... 8 rows omitted in the middle; use print(x, n = Inf) to show all rows.

The .merge column records match status. Use dplyr joins for ordinary joins; stata_merge() is useful when you also want Stata-style match reporting and checks.

Follow participants over time

A later survey creates a panel. Participant 1 misses wave 2: the change from the previous wave should therefore be missing at wave 3.

followup <- tribble(
  ~id, ~wave, ~score,
    1,     1,      3,
    1,     3,      7,
    2,     1,      4,
    2,     2,      6
)

followup |>
  isid(id, wave) |>
  mutate(
    previous = stata_lag(score, time = wave),
    change = stata_diff(score, time = wave),
    .by = id
  )
#> Variables `id`, `wave` together uniquely identify the rows.
#> # A tibble: 4 × 5
#>      id  wave score previous change
#>   <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>    <dbl>  <dbl>
#> 1     1     1     3       NA     NA
#> 2     1     3     7       NA     NA
#> 3     2     1     4       NA     NA
#> 4     2     2     6        4      2

These helpers find the previous period, whereas dplyr::lag() finds the previous row. stata_lead() looks ahead by period. Always identify the panel in .by or group_by().

Keep exploring

Use category tables to compare responses and measurement summaries to compare scores and incomes. preview() controls a table’s continuing display, while print_headtail() and print_interval() print it briefly once; all retain the complete data. See the conventions guide for details.

For occasional workflow tasks, the reference covers reproducible draws with set_seed(), timing with timer(), and continuing after an optional expression fails with capture(). To find a familiar Stata operation, try findit("tab satisfied"); editor and clipboard helpers are also available.
